Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১) What is the appropriate process for sterilization of culture media containing serum/egg?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Tyndallization (fractional sterilization) is the appropriate method for sterilizing culture media containing serum or egg, because these components are heat-labile and may be damaged by autoclaving.

Tyndallization involves intermittent steaming at 100°C for 20–30 minutes on successive days, allowing spores to germinate between heating cycles and then be destroyed.

Other options:

  • Autoclaving → uses high temperature (121°C) and may coagulate/damage serum or egg-containing media.

  • Steaming → single exposure is insufficient for spores.

  • Hot air oven → used for dry materials like glassware, oils, and powders.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Serum/egg-containing media → Tyndallization

  • Autoclave → 121°C, 15 psi, 15–20 min

  • Hot air oven → dry heat sterilization

  • Filtration → heat-sensitive fluids

Exam Pearl:
Heat-sensitive culture media containing serum or egg are sterilized by Tyndallization.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২) If ATS is given, what type of immunity is achieved?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
ATS (Anti-Tetanus Serum) provides passive artificial immunity because it contains preformed antibodies (antitoxin) obtained from an external source and gives immediate but temporary protection.

  • Passive → ready-made antibodies are administered.

  • Artificial → antibodies are given through medical intervention (injection).

Other options:

  • Active natural → immunity after natural infection.

  • Active artificial → vaccination (e.g., tetanus toxoid vaccine).

  • Passive natural → maternal antibodies through placenta or breast milk.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ATS / immunoglobulin → Passive artificial immunity

  • Vaccines → Active artificial immunity

  • Maternal IgG → Passive natural immunity

  • Infection → Active natural immunity

Exam Pearl:
Antibody injection (ATS) = passive artificial immunity.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩) Traumatic fat necrosis occurs in......?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Traumatic fat necrosis most commonly occurs in the breast. It is a benign inflammatory process caused by injury to breast tissue, leading to damage of fat cells, fat breakdown, inflammation, and fibrosis. It may clinically mimic breast carcinoma as a lump.

Other options:

  • Kidney → not a typical site of traumatic fat necrosis.

  • Brain → trauma may cause other forms of injury, but not typical fat necrosis.

  • Liver → not a common site.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Traumatic fat necrosis → Breast

  • Presents as:

    • Palpable breast lump

    • May have skin changes

    • Can mimic malignancy

  • Common causes:

    • Blunt trauma

    • Surgery

    • Radiotherapy

Exam Pearl:
A breast lump after trauma = consider traumatic fat necrosis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪) Which is not a feature of primary immune response?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The primary immune response occurs after the first exposure to an antigen. It is characterized by a longer latent period and initially produces IgM antibodies, followed by smaller amounts of IgG. Therefore, IgG dominant response is not a feature of primary immune response; it is a feature of the secondary immune response.

Other options:

  • Long latent period → Feature of primary response (slow antibody production)

  • No memory cell → Primary response generates memory cells (but the response is not dependent on pre-existing memory cells)

  • 1st exposure → Definition of primary immune response

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Feature Primary Response Secondary Response
Exposure First exposure Subsequent exposure
Main antibody IgM IgG
Latent period Long Short
Antibody level Low High
Memory cells Formed Activated

Exam Pearl:
Primary immune response = first exposure + IgM predominant + long lag phase.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫) Brodie abscess is a consequence of…..?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Brodie abscess is a type of subacute osteomyelitis, which is considered a localized form of chronic osteomyelitis. It is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus and presents as a localized abscess within bone, commonly affecting the metaphysis of long bones (especially the tibia).

Other options:

  • Acute osteomyelitis → causes rapid bone infection with systemic features, not typically Brodie abscess.

  • Giant cell tumor → benign bone tumor, usually in epiphysis.

  • Ewing’s sarcoma → malignant bone tumor of children/young adults, usually diaphysis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Brodie abscess → Subacute/chronic osteomyelitis

  • Common organism → Staphylococcus aureus

  • Common site → Metaphysis of long bones

  • X-ray → Lytic lesion with surrounding sclerosis

Exam Pearl:
Brodie abscess is a localized abscess of subacute (chronic) osteomyelitis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬) Cellular shape & architecture is preserved in.......?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
In coagulative necrosis, the cellular shape and tissue architecture are preserved for several days despite cell death. This occurs because protein denaturation inhibits proteolysis, maintaining the basic outline of cells and tissues.

It is typically seen in ischemic infarction of solid organs (except the brain).

Other options:

  • Fat necrosis → destruction of fat cells with fatty acid release and calcium soap formation (saponification).

  • Caseous necrosis → loss of tissue architecture with cheese-like appearance, classically in tuberculosis.

  • Liquefactive necrosis → complete digestion of cells producing a liquid cavity (e.g., brain infarct, abscess).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Coagulative necrosis → Architecture preserved

  • Liquefactive necrosis → Architecture lost

  • Caseous necrosis → TB, cheese-like appearance

  • Fat necrosis → Pancreatitis, breast trauma

Exam Pearl:
Preserved cellular architecture after cell death = Coagulative necrosis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭) Which is example of type-2 hypersensitivity reaction?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Type II hypersensitivity reaction is an antibody-mediated (IgG or IgM) cytotoxic reaction where antibodies bind to antigens on cell surfaces or extracellular matrix, causing cell destruction or dysfunction.

Transfusion reaction (especially incompatible blood transfusion) is a classic example of Type II hypersensitivity due to IgM antibodies against RBC antigens, leading to complement-mediated hemolysis.

Other options:

  • Bronchial asthma → Type I hypersensitivity (IgE-mediated)

  • TB → Type IV hypersensitivity (T-cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity)

  • Rheumatoid arthritis → Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex-mediated)

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Type Mechanism Examples
Type I IgE-mediated Asthma, anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis
Type II IgG/IgM against cell surface Transfusion reaction, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome
Type III Immune complex deposition SLE, RA, serum sickness
Type IV T-cell mediated TB, contact dermatitis

Exam Pearl:
ABO incompatible transfusion reaction = Type II hypersensitivity.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮) Which enzyme is elevated in prostatic disease?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) is elevated in prostatic diseases, particularly carcinoma of the prostate, especially when there is metastatic disease.

  • Acid phosphatase (PAP) → classically associated with prostate

  • Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) → elevated in bone and hepatobiliary disease; may rise in prostate cancer with bone metastasis

  • GGT → hepatobiliary disease

  • LDH → tissue injury, hemolysis, malignancy, etc.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Prostate → Acid phosphatase

  • Bone → Alkaline phosphatase

  • Liver/bile ducts → GGT

  • Modern screening for prostate cancer → PSA, not PAP

Exam Pearl:
Classic enzyme marker of prostatic disease = Acid phosphatase (PAP).

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৯) Where adaptive change of tissue occurs?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Metaplasia is a reversible adaptive change in which one mature, differentiated cell type is replaced by another mature cell type better able to tolerate a persistent stress or stimulus.

Examples:

  • Bronchial epithelium: columnar → stratified squamous epithelium in smokers

  • Barrett esophagus: squamous → intestinal-type columnar epithelium due to chronic reflux

Other options:

  • Metastasis → spread of malignant tumor to distant sites.

  • Dysplasia → abnormal cellular growth and maturation; may be premalignant.

  • Neoplasia → abnormal autonomous proliferation of cells.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adaptive cellular changes: hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia

  • Metaplasia → reversible

  • Dysplasia → potentially premalignant

Exam Pearl:
Adaptive replacement of one mature cell type by another = Metaplasia.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১০) Where physiological atrophy occurs?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Physiological atrophy is a normal, programmed decrease in the size of a tissue or organ after it has fulfilled its physiological function.

After parturition (childbirth), the enlarged uterus undergoes physiological involution/atrophy and gradually returns toward its normal size.

Other options are examples of pathological atrophy:

  • Marasmus → nutritional atrophy due to severe malnutrition.

  • Atrophy of disuse → due to decreased physical activity.

  • Cancer cachexia → systemic wasting associated with malignancy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Physiological atrophy → Uterine involution after parturition

  • Disuse atrophy → reduced workload

  • Nutritional atrophy → malnutrition

  • Cachexia → chronic disease/malignancy

Exam Pearl:
Uterus after childbirth → physiological atrophy (involution).

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১১) Which subtype of rhabdomyosarcoma is predominant?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common subtype of rhabdomyosarcoma, particularly in children. It commonly arises in the head and neck region and genitourinary tract.

Other options:

  • Alveolar → more common in older children/adolescents; often involves extremities.

  • Pleomorphic → rare, usually occurs in adults.

  • Medullary → not a recognized major subtype of rhabdomyosarcoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common RMS → Embryonal

  • Children → Embryonal

  • Adolescents → Alveolar

  • Adults → Pleomorphic

Exam Pearl:
Rhabdomyosarcoma in a child → think Embryonal subtype.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১২) What is the normal value of reticulocyte?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The normal reticulocyte count in adults is approximately 0.5–2% of circulating RBCs. Among the given options, 0.2–2.0% is the best answer.

Reticulocytes are immature RBCs recently released from the bone marrow. The reticulocyte count is useful for assessing bone marrow erythropoietic activity.

  • ↑ Reticulocyte count → increased RBC production, e.g. hemolysis or acute blood loss.

  • ↓ Reticulocyte count → reduced marrow production, e.g. iron deficiency, aplastic anemia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Normal reticulocyte count → ~0.5–2%

  • Hemolysis → Reticulocytes ↑

  • Aplastic anemia → Reticulocytes ↓

  • Reticulocytes reflect marrow response to anemia

Exam Pearl:
Normal reticulocyte count ≈ 0.5–2%; among the options → 0.2–2.0%.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১৩) Pappenheimer bodies are found in---?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing granules within RBCs, representing abnormal accumulation of ferritin/iron in mitochondria. They are characteristically seen in sideroblastic anemia.

They can also be seen in other conditions such as post-splenectomy states, but sideroblastic anemia is the classic exam association.

  • Megaloblastic anemia → Howell–Jolly bodies, hypersegmented neutrophils

  • Sideroblastic anemia → Pappenheimer bodies, ring sideroblasts in bone marrow

  • Hemolytic anemia → reticulocytosis, polychromasia

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Inclusion Classic association
Pappenheimer bodies Sideroblastic anemia
Howell–Jolly bodies Post-splenectomy / hyposplenism
Heinz bodies G6PD deficiency
Basophilic stippling Lead poisoning
Cabot rings Megaloblastic anemia

Exam Pearl:
Pappenheimer bodies = iron granules → Sideroblastic anemia.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১৪) Where pathological hypertrophy occurs?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.option4: hypertrophy of skeletal muscles in body builder
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Pathological hypertrophy is an increase in the size of cells due to abnormal/chronic stress, resulting in enlargement of the affected organ.

Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) occurs in conditions such as chronic hypertension or aortic stenosis due to increased workload on the heart. It is a classic example of pathological hypertrophy.

Other options are examples of physiological hypertrophy:

  • Pregnant uterus → physiological hypertrophy due to hormonal stimulation.

  • Breast during lactation → mainly physiological hyperplasia with hypertrophic changes.

  • Skeletal muscles in bodybuilders → physiological hypertrophy due to increased workload.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pathological hypertrophy → LVH in hypertension/aortic stenosis

  • Physiological hypertrophy → skeletal muscle in exercise

  • Physiological uterine hypertrophy → pregnancy

Exam Pearl:
Chronic pressure overload → LVH → classic pathological hypertrophy.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১৫) Which is not an absolute indication for bone marrow aspiration?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Bone marrow aspiration (BMA) is not routinely required in typical ITP. ITP is primarily a clinical diagnosis characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia with otherwise normal blood findings. Bone marrow examination is considered when the presentation is atypical or another hematological disorder is suspected.

Bone marrow examination is important/indicated in:

  • Aplastic anemia → assesses marrow cellularity and confirms hypocellular marrow.

  • Multiple myeloma → demonstrates clonal plasma-cell proliferation.

  • Lymphoma → may be performed for bone marrow involvement/staging.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Typical ITP → BMA usually not required

  • Aplastic anemia → hypocellular marrow

  • Multiple myeloma → increased clonal plasma cells

  • Lymphoma → marrow examination for staging/involvement

Exam Pearl:
Typical ITP does not require routine bone marrow aspiration.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১৬) Which histological type of primary bone tumor are predominant?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Chondrogenic tumors are the predominant histological type of primary bone tumors. This group includes tumors such as osteochondroma, enchondroma, and chondrosarcoma.

Other options:

  • Hemopoietic → includes tumors such as plasmacytoma/multiple myeloma involving bone.

  • Osteogenic → includes osteoma and osteosarcoma, but is less common overall.

  • Fibrogenic → includes fibrous tumors of bone, which are less common.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common histological group of primary bone tumors → Chondrogenic

  • Common benign cartilage tumor → Osteochondroma

  • Common malignant cartilage tumor → Chondrosarcoma

  • Common malignant osteogenic tumor → Osteosarcoma

Exam Pearl:
Primary bone tumors → Chondrogenic type predominates.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১৭) Where compensatory hyperplasia occurs?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Compensatory hyperplasia occurs when a portion of an organ is removed or damaged, causing the remaining cells to proliferate to restore the organ's functional mass.

A classic example is liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy. Hepatocytes undergo controlled proliferation to restore liver mass.

Other options:

  • Pregnant uterus → hormonal hyperplasia + hypertrophy.

  • Female breast → hormonal/physiological hyperplasia during pregnancy.

  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) → pathological hormonal hyperplasia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Compensatory hyperplasia → Liver after partial hepatectomy

  • Hormonal hyperplasia → Endometrium, breast during pregnancy

  • Pathological hyperplasia → BPH, endometrial hyperplasia

Exam Pearl:
Partial removal of liver → compensatory hyperplasia/regeneration.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১৮) Schilling test is done for the assessment of which deficiency?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The Schilling test was historically used to assess vitamin B12 absorption and help determine the cause of vitamin B12 deficiency, particularly whether deficiency was due to intrinsic factor deficiency (pernicious anemia) or malabsorption.

The test uses radiolabeled vitamin B12 and measures its urinary excretion after administration.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Schilling test → Vitamin B12 absorption

  • Pernicious anemia → Intrinsic factor deficiency

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency → Megaloblastic anemia + neurological manifestations

  • Folic acid deficiency → No neurological manifestations

Exam Pearl:
Schilling test = Vitamin B12 absorption/deficiency.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ১৯) Where connective tissue metaplasia occurs?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Myositis ossificans is a classic example of connective tissue metaplasia, where fibroblasts within connective tissue differentiate into bone-forming cells, producing mature bone in soft tissue.

Other options are examples of epithelial metaplasia:

  • Bile duct obstruction → may cause squamous metaplasia.

  • Habitual smoker → respiratory columnar epithelium → stratified squamous epithelium.

  • Barrett esophagus → squamous epithelium → intestinal-type columnar epithelium.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Connective tissue → bone/cartilage = Myositis ossificans

  • Smoker → Squamous metaplasia

  • Barrett esophagus → Intestinal metaplasia

  • Metaplasia → generally reversible adaptive change

Exam Pearl:
Connective tissue metaplasia → Myositis ossificans.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২০) Which endogenous pigment accumulates inside the cell?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Lipofuscin is an endogenous pigment that accumulates inside cells, particularly in long-lived cells such as cardiac myocytes and neurons. It is a yellow-brown pigment formed from lipid-containing residues of lysosomal digestion and is associated with aging (“wear-and-tear pigment”).

Other options:

  • Carbon dust / coal dust → exogenous pigment, causes anthracosis.

  • Aniline → exogenous pigment/toxin, not a normal endogenous pigment.

  • Lipofuscin → endogenous intracellular pigment.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Lipofuscin → endogenous → aging

  • Melanin → endogenous pigment

  • Hemosiderin → endogenous iron-storage pigment

  • Carbon → exogenous pigment → anthracosis

Exam Pearl:
Intracellular endogenous “wear-and-tear” pigment = Lipofuscin.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২১) Infiltration of epidermis by inflammatory cells is called….?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
In dermatopathology, exocytosis refers to the migration/infiltration of inflammatory cells from the dermis into the epidermis.

Other options:

  • Erosion → superficial loss of epidermis.

  • Ulceration → loss of epidermis extending into the dermis or deeper tissue.

  • Acanthosis → thickening of the epidermis, mainly due to increased thickness of the stratum spinosum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Exocytosis → inflammatory cells enter epidermis

  • Acanthosis → epidermal thickening

  • Erosion → superficial epidermal loss

  • Ulcer → deeper tissue loss

Exam Pearl:
Inflammatory cell infiltration into the epidermis = Exocytosis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২২) Which one is most common site of fatty change?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The liver is the most common site of fatty change (fatty degeneration/steatosis) because it plays a central role in lipid metabolism. Excess triglycerides accumulate within hepatocytes when lipid uptake, synthesis, oxidation, or export is disturbed.

Common causes include:

  • Alcohol

  • Obesity/metabolic syndrome

  • Diabetes mellitus

  • Protein malnutrition

  • Certain drugs/toxins

Other organs can develop lipid accumulation, but liver is the classic and most common site.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common site of fatty change → Liver

  • Fatty liver → triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes

  • Alcohol is a major cause

Exam Pearl:
Fatty change = think liver first.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২৩) Disorders producing paraproteinaemia excludes…?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Paraproteinaemia refers to the presence of a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) in the blood, usually produced by a clonal B-cell or plasma-cell disorder.

  • Multiple myeloma → classic cause; monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains.

  • CLL → can be associated with monoclonal gammopathy/paraproteinaemia.

  • Primary amyloidosis (AL amyloidosis) → associated with a plasma-cell clone producing monoclonal light chains.

  • Hodgkin’s lymphoma → not a typical cause of paraproteinaemia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Multiple myeloma → M-protein

  • Waldenström macroglobulinaemia → IgM paraprotein

  • AL amyloidosis → monoclonal light chains

  • Hodgkin lymphoma → not classically associated

Exam Pearl:
Paraproteinaemia → think plasma-cell/B-cell disorders; Hodgkin lymphoma is the exception here.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২৪) Which one is site of metastatic calcification?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Metastatic calcification occurs in otherwise normal tissues due to hypercalcemia and/or hyperphosphatemia. Common sites include the gastric mucosa, kidneys, lungs, and systemic arteries.

  • Gastric mucosa → classic site of metastatic calcification.

  • Heart valve → commonly associated with dystrophic calcification.

  • Necrotic tissue → dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged/dead tissues.

  • Dead parasites → can undergo dystrophic calcification.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Type Serum Ca²⁺ Tissue Examples
Metastatic Usually ↑ Normal tissue Gastric mucosa, kidney, lung
Dystrophic Usually normal Damaged/necrotic tissue Valves, atherosclerotic plaques, dead parasites

Exam Pearl:
Metastatic calcification → normal tissue + hypercalcemia → gastric mucosa is a classic site.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২৫) Leukemia is associated with which of the following genetic disease?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is strongly associated with an increased risk of leukemia, particularly acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML)—especially acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL/M7) in children.

Other options are not classically associated with a major increased leukemia risk:

  • Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18) → severe congenital abnormalities.

  • Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13) → severe congenital abnormalities.

  • Turner syndrome (45,X) → short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, etc.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Down syndrome → ↑ leukemia risk

  • Down + AML → especially megakaryoblastic (AMKL)

  • Down + childhood leukemia → ALL and AML

Exam Pearl:
Leukemia + chromosomal syndrome → think Down syndrome (Trisomy 21).

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২৬) Which is a premalignant epidermal tumor?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Actinic keratosis is a premalignant epidermal lesion caused by chronic ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure. It can progress to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).

Other options:

  • Acanthosis nigricans → epidermal thickening, commonly associated with insulin resistance or malignancy; not a premalignant epidermal tumor.

  • Paget’s disease → malignant disease involving the nipple/epidermis, usually associated with underlying breast carcinoma.

  • Keratoacanthoma → rapidly growing keratinizing lesion; historically considered a low-grade variant of SCC, but not the classic answer for premalignant epidermal lesion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Actinic keratosis → premalignant → SCC

  • Cause → chronic UV exposure

  • Common sites → sun-exposed skin

  • Histology → atypical keratinocytes

Exam Pearl:
Premalignant epidermal lesion = Actinic keratosis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২৭) Which is caused by chronic inflammatory reaction?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Chronic inflammatory reactions are characterized by persistent inflammation, with lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells, along with tissue destruction and attempts at repair.

Arthritis, particularly chronic inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis, is a classic example of a disease caused by chronic inflammation.

Other options:

  • ARDS → acute inflammatory lung injury.

  • Septic shock → acute systemic inflammatory response to infection.

  • Glomerulonephritis → commonly mediated by immune mechanisms; many forms are acute or immune-complex mediated rather than a classic chronic inflammatory reaction.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Chronic inflammation → RA, chronic infections, TB

  • Main cells → lymphocytes + macrophages + plasma cells

  • Acute inflammation → neutrophils, edema, vascular changes

Exam Pearl:
Chronic inflammatory disease → Rheumatoid arthritis is a classic example.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২৮) Which one is a feature of transudate?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
A transudate is a fluid that accumulates due to non-inflammatory mechanisms, mainly changes in hydrostatic pressure or plasma oncotic pressure. It typically has low protein content and few cells.

Transudate examples include effusions due to congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome.

Other options describe exudate:

  • Plenty of polymorphs → inflammatory exudate

  • Tendency to clot → exudate has more fibrinogen

  • High plasma protein → exudate

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Feature Transudate Exudate
Cause Non-inflammatory Inflammatory
Protein Low High
Cells Few Many
Fibrinogen Low High
Clotting Usually absent May clot

Exam Pearl:
Transudate = non-inflammatory, low-protein fluid.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ২৯) INR is used to assess the therapeutic effect of--?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
INR (International Normalized Ratio) is used to monitor the therapeutic effect of coumarin anticoagulants, especially warfarin.

Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing synthesis of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. Its effect is monitored using PT, which is standardized as INR.

Other options:

  • LMW heparin → monitored mainly by anti-factor Xa when monitoring is needed.

  • Unfractionated (HMW) heparin → aPTT is traditionally used.

  • Streptokinase → thrombolytic; INR is not used to monitor its therapeutic effect.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Warfarin/Coumarin → PT/INR

  • Unfractionated heparin → aPTT

  • LMWH → anti-Xa

  • Direct oral anticoagulants → routine INR monitoring not required

Exam Pearl:
PT/INR = monitor warfarin (coumarin) therapy.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩০) Emigration of leukocyte to the site of injury is called……?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Diapedesis (transmigration) is the process by which leukocytes move out of the bloodstream through the endothelial wall and enter the surrounding tissue at the site of injury or inflammation.

  • Rolling → leukocytes loosely attach and roll along the endothelium, mainly via selectins.

  • Diapedesis → leukocytes cross the endothelial barrier; mainly mediated by PECAM-1 (CD31).

  • Chemotaxis → directed movement of leukocytes toward the chemical gradient after leaving the vessel.

  • Phagocytosis → engulfment and digestion of pathogens/debris.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  1. Margination

  2. Rolling → Selectins

  3. Adhesion → Integrins

  4. Diapedesis → PECAM-1

  5. Chemotaxis

  6. Phagocytosis

Exam Pearl:
Leukocyte crossing the vessel wall = Diapedesis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩১) Clinical triad of Graves’ disease excludes….?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The classic clinical triad of Graves’ disease consists of:

  1. Hyperthyroidism

  2. Ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease)

  3. Infiltrative dermopathy — especially pretibial myxedema

Infiltrative myopathy is not a component of the classic triad.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Graves’ disease → Hyperthyroidism + Ophthalmopathy + Dermopathy

  • Ophthalmopathy → proptosis, lid retraction, diplopia

  • Dermopathy → pretibial myxedema

  • Thyroid acropachy may occur in severe cases

Exam Pearl:
Graves’ triad = Hyperthyroidism + Ophthalmopathy + Dermopathy → “myopathy” is the exception.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩২) Which one is the most important test for recent infection with HBV?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
IgM anti-HBc (IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen) is the most important serological marker of recent/acute HBV infection. It usually appears early during acute infection and generally persists for several months.

  • IgM anti-HBc → recent/acute infection

  • IgG anti-HBc → previous or chronic infection

  • Anti-HBe → seroconversion/low viral replication, not the main marker of recent infection.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Marker Significance
HBsAg Current HBV infection
IgM anti-HBc Recent/acute infection
IgG anti-HBc Previous/chronic infection
Anti-HBs Immunity
HBeAg High infectivity/viral replication

Exam Pearl:
Recent HBV infection → IgM anti-HBc.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩৩) Which is dominant cellular player in chronic inflammation?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The macrophage is the dominant cellular player in chronic inflammation. Macrophages are derived from circulating monocytes and play a central role in both tissue injury and repair by releasing cytokines, growth factors, and inflammatory mediators.

Other options:

  • Plasma cells → prominent in some chronic inflammatory conditions but not the dominant cell overall.

  • Eosinophils → prominent in parasitic infections and allergic reactions.

  • Neutrophils → predominantly associated with acute inflammation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Acute inflammation → Neutrophils

  • Chronic inflammation → Macrophages + lymphocytes + plasma cells

  • Macrophages → cytokine production, phagocytosis, tissue repair

Exam Pearl:
Dominant cell in chronic inflammation = Macrophage.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩৪) Which disease is caused by clostridium perfringens?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Clostridium perfringens causes food poisoning, typically after ingestion of contaminated meat or meat products. It produces enterotoxin, causing abdominal cramps and diarrhea, usually within 6–24 hours.

Other options:

  • Tetanus → Clostridium tetani

  • Botulism → Clostridium botulinum

  • Pseudomembranous colitis → Clostridioides difficile

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Clostridium Classic disease
C. perfringens Food poisoning, gas gangrene
C. tetani Tetanus
C. botulinum Botulism
C. difficile Pseudomembranous colitis

Exam Pearl:
C. perfringens → food poisoning + gas gangrene.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩৫) What is the desired change in CBC in Asthma?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Eosinophilia is a classic hematological finding in allergic/atopic bronchial asthma, reflecting type 2 (Th2) inflammation and increased eosinophilic activity. Eosinophils contribute to airway inflammation through mediators such as major basic protein and leukotrienes.

Other options:

  • Monocytosis → not a typical finding in asthma.

  • Neutrophilia → may occur during infection or corticosteroid therapy, but is not the classic asthma finding.

  • Lymphopenia → not characteristic of asthma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Asthma → Eosinophilia

  • Allergic asthma → ↑ IgE, eosinophils, FeNO

  • Eosinophils → important in Type 2 airway inflammation

Exam Pearl:
Asthma + CBC → think eosinophilia.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩৬) Clinical triad of Meig’s syndrome excludes….?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Meigs syndrome is classically defined by the triad of:

  1. Ovarian fibroma (benign ovarian tumor)

  2. Ascites

  3. Pleural effusion

The pleural effusion is often right-sided and typically resolves after removal of the ovarian tumor.

  • Malignant ovarian tumor → not part of the classic Meigs triad.

  • Ascites → present.

  • Pleural effusion → present.

  • Fibroma of ovary → essential component.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Meigs syndrome = Ovarian fibroma + Ascites + Pleural effusion

  • Pseudo-Meigs → associated with other ovarian tumors, e.g. ovarian teratoma.

  • Meigs tumor is benign, not malignant.

Exam Pearl:
Meigs = Fibroma + Ascites + Pleural effusion.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩৭) What is the shape of capsid of rabies virus?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The rabies virus has a characteristic bullet-shaped (or bullet-like) virion. It belongs to the Rhabdoviridae family, and the name Rhabdo refers to a rod-shaped appearance.

  • Rabies virus → Bullet-shaped

  • It is an enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus.

  • The nucleocapsid has a helical symmetry.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Virus Characteristic shape
Rabies Bullet
Poxvirus Brick
Adenovirus Icosahedral
Bacteriophage Tadpole

Exam Pearl:
Rabies virus = bullet-shaped virion.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩৮) Opsonization greatly enhance -
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Opsonization is the process of coating a pathogen with opsonins such as IgG and C3b, making it easier for phagocytes to recognize and engulf it.

Opsonized microbes bind to specific receptors on phagocytes:

  • IgG → Fc receptors

  • C3b → complement receptors

This greatly enhances phagocytosis.

Other options:

  • Chemotaxis → directed movement toward chemical signals.

  • Margination → leukocytes move toward the endothelial surface.

  • Diapedesis → leukocytes cross the vessel wall.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Opsonization → ↑ Phagocytosis

  • Major opsonins → IgG, C3b

  • C3b receptor → complement receptor on phagocytes

Exam Pearl:
Opsonization makes phagocytosis easier and more efficient.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৩৯) Which group of streptococcus is leading cause of neonatal sepsis?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Streptococcus agalactiae, also called Group B Streptococcus (GBS), is a major cause of neonatal sepsis, particularly early-onset neonatal sepsis. It is commonly colonized in the maternal genital and gastrointestinal tracts and can be transmitted to the newborn during delivery.

Other options:

  • S. viridans → mainly dental/oral flora; associated with subacute endocarditis.

  • S. pyogenes (Group A) → pharyngitis, skin infections, rheumatic fever.

  • S. faecalis (Enterococcus faecalis) → healthcare-associated infections, UTI, endocarditis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Neonatal sepsis/meningitis → Group B Strep (S. agalactiae)

  • Maternal genital colonization → important risk factor

  • GBS screening in pregnancy helps prevent neonatal disease.

Exam Pearl:
Neonatal sepsis + Streptococcus → think Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae).

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪০) Where ROS are produced?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are produced physiologically in several cellular locations, but the mitochondria are a major source. During oxidative phosphorylation, electrons can leak from the electron transport chain and react with oxygen, generating ROS such as superoxide (O₂⁻).

Other sources include peroxisomes and the endoplasmic reticulum, but among the given options, mitochondria is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Major ROS source → Mitochondrial electron transport chain

  • ROS → superoxide, H₂O₂, hydroxyl radical

  • ROS can cause lipid peroxidation, protein damage, and DNA damage

Exam Pearl:
ROS → mainly generated during mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪১) Which is most dangerous tumor of kidney?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (clear cell RCC) is the most common and classically the most important/malignant primary renal cell carcinoma. It has a strong tendency for vascular invasion and hematogenous metastasis, particularly to the lungs, bones, liver, and brain.

  • Clear cell carcinoma → most common RCC; potentially aggressive with early vascular spread.

  • Papillary carcinoma → generally less aggressive, though type 2 can be aggressive.

  • Urothelial carcinoma → arises from the renal pelvis/urothelium, not renal parenchyma.

  • Collecting duct carcinoma → rare and highly aggressive, but much less common.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common RCC → Clear cell

  • Clear cell RCC → VHL gene association

  • Most common route of spread → hematogenous

  • RCC may extend into renal vein → IVC

Exam Pearl:
Kidney tumor + most common/major aggressive RCC → Clear cell carcinoma.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪২) Which one is second week symptom of enteric fever?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Rose spots are a characteristic feature of enteric (typhoid) fever that typically appear during the second week of illness. They are small, rose-colored, blanching macules, mainly seen on the trunk and upper abdomen.

Other options:

  • Myalgia → may occur early but is nonspecific.

  • Relative bradycardia → can occur in typhoid fever but is not specifically a second-week feature.

  • Constipation → may occur early, especially in adults; diarrhea may occur later.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • 1st week → fever, headache, malaise, abdominal symptoms

  • 2nd week → rose spots, hepatosplenomegaly, relative bradycardia

  • 3rd week → intestinal complications such as hemorrhage/perforation

Exam Pearl:
Enteric fever + 2nd week + trunk rash = Rose spots.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪৩) What are the principal source of leukotrienes?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Mast cells are a principal cellular source of leukotrienes, which are synthesized from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway.

Leukotrienes, especially LTC₄, LTD₄, and LTE₄, cause:

  • Bronchoconstriction

  • Increased vascular permeability

  • Increased mucus secretion

They are particularly important in bronchial asthma and allergic inflammation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Mast cell → Leukotrienes

  • Arachidonic acid → 5-lipoxygenase → Leukotrienes

  • LTC₄/LTD₄/LTE₄ → bronchoconstriction

  • LTB₄ → neutrophil chemotaxis

Exam Pearl:
Leukotrienes → principal source: mast cells → potent bronchoconstrictors.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪৪) Which is not a cardinal features of Hansen's disease?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.option3: acid fast bacilli on skin smears
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The cardinal features of Hansen’s disease (leprosy) used for diagnosis include:

  1. Definite loss of sensation in a skin lesion

  2. Thickened peripheral nerve with sensory/motor loss

  3. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) demonstrated in a slit-skin smear

Although Hansen’s disease is indeed caused by Mycobacterium leprae, this is the etiological cause, not one of the classic cardinal clinical/laboratory features.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Skin lesion + sensory loss → cardinal sign

  • Thickened peripheral nerve → cardinal sign

  • AFB in skin smear → cardinal sign

  • Causative organism → M. leprae

Exam Pearl:
Leprosy cardinal signs = sensory loss + thickened nerve + AFB; organism itself is not a cardinal feature.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪৫) All are the functions of complement except……?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The complement system is part of innate and adaptive immune defense and has several important functions:

  • Cell lysis → mainly through the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b–C9)

  • Opsonization → mainly C3b, enhancing phagocytosis

  • Chemotaxis → especially C5a, which attracts neutrophils

  • Antigen production → not a function of complement

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • C3b → Opsonization

  • C5a → Chemotaxis + inflammation

  • C5b–C9 → Cell lysis (MAC)

  • C3a/C5a → Anaphylatoxins

Exam Pearl:
Complement does lysis, opsonization and chemotaxis—but does NOT produce antigen.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪৬) Which is the most frequent primary tumor of pediatric heart?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Cardiac rhabdomyoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in children. It is usually benign and commonly arises within the ventricular myocardium. Multiple rhabdomyomas are strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis complex.

Other options:

  • Myxoma → most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, usually in the left atrium.

  • Fibroma → second most common primary cardiac tumor in children; usually solitary and intramural.

  • Lipoma → rare in children.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Children → Rhabdomyoma

  • Adults → Myxoma

  • Rhabdomyoma → strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis

  • Pediatric cardiac tumors → usually benign

Exam Pearl:
Most common primary cardiac tumor in children = Rhabdomyoma.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪৭) Which one is the most important diagnostic method in enteric fever?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Blood culture is the most important and definitive diagnostic test for enteric (typhoid) fever, particularly during the first week of illness. It can directly demonstrate Salmonella Typhi or S. Paratyphi.

  • Blood culture → Gold standard/definitive diagnosis, especially early disease.

  • Widal test → less specific and less reliable; may become positive after the first week.

  • Urine culture → lower sensitivity and not the primary diagnostic test.

  • CBC → nonspecific; may show leukopenia but cannot confirm typhoid.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • 1st week → Blood culture

  • Later weeks → Stool culture becomes more useful

  • Widal → supportive only; significant limitations

Exam Pearl:
Enteric fever → Blood culture is the key diagnostic test.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪৮) Caseating granuloma occurs in-
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
A caseating granuloma is classically associated with tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It consists of a central area of caseous necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes.

  • TB → caseating granuloma ✅

  • Leprosy → granulomas may occur, but typically non-caseating, especially in tuberculoid leprosy.

  • Sarcoidosis → non-caseating granulomas.

  • Syphilis → gummatous lesions can occur in tertiary disease but caseating granuloma is not the classic finding.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Caseating granuloma → TB

  • Non-caseating granuloma → Sarcoidosis

  • Tuberculoid leprosy → well-formed non-caseating granulomas

  • Langhans giant cells → classically seen in TB granulomas

Exam Pearl:
Caseation = TB until proven otherwise.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৪৯) Following conditions are favorable for healing by primary intention except…..?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Explanation:
Healing by primary intention occurs when the wound edges are closely approximated, with minimal tissue loss and little contamination. This results in relatively rapid healing with a small scar.

  • No loss of tissue → favorable 

  • Minimum loss of tissue → favorable 

  • Approximated edges → favorable 

  • Large defect → unfavorable ; usually requires healing by secondary intention.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Primary intention: clean wound + approximated edges + minimal tissue loss → small scar.

  • Secondary intention: large tissue defect + wound left open → more granulation tissue and larger scar.

Exam Pearl:
Primary intention = closely apposed wound edges; large defect is the exception.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫০) Which is not a viral cause of acute watery diarrhoea?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The major viral causes of acute watery diarrhea include:

  • Rotavirus → major cause in infants and young children.

  • Adenovirus (enteric types 40, 41) → causes gastroenteritis, especially in children.

  • Astrovirus → causes acute gastroenteritis, particularly in young children.

  • “Archi virus” → not a recognized viral cause of acute watery diarrhea.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Rotavirus → severe watery diarrhea in infants

  • Norovirus → common cause of outbreaks in all age groups

  • Enteric adenovirus 40/41 → pediatric gastroenteritis

  • Astrovirus → pediatric gastroenteritis

Exam Pearl:
Acute watery diarrhea viruses → Rota, Noro, Adeno, Astro. “Archi virus” is the exception.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫১) Which is not a physiological cause of proteinuria?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Physiological/transient proteinuria can occur without intrinsic renal disease. Recognized causes include:

  • Orthostatic proteinuria → especially in adolescents.

  • Exercise-induced proteinuria → transient after strenuous exercise.

  • Exposure to cold → can cause transient proteinuria.

Sleep is not a recognized physiological cause of proteinuria.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Physiological/transient proteinuria → exercise, fever, cold exposure, orthostatic state

  • Orthostatic proteinuria → typically young, otherwise healthy individuals

  • Persistent proteinuria → consider renal disease

Exam Pearl:
Physiological proteinuria → think exercise, cold, fever, orthostatic—not sleep.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫২) Features of granulation tissue excludes….?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The common viral causes of acute watery diarrhoea include:

  • Rotavirus → important cause of severe diarrhea in infants and young children.

  • Adenovirus (40, 41) → causes acute gastroenteritis.

  • Astrovirus → causes watery diarrhea, especially in children.

  • “Archi virus” → not a recognized cause of acute watery diarrhea.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Rotavirus → children

  • Norovirus → outbreaks, all age groups

  • Enteric adenovirus 40/41 → gastroenteritis

  • Astrovirus → pediatric gastroenteritis

Exam Pearl:
Rota + Noro + Adeno + Astro → viral acute watery diarrhea.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫৩) Which is not a component of Ghon's complex?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Ghon’s complex is the primary complex of tuberculosis, consisting of:

  • Ghon focus → primary parenchymal lesion

  • Lymphangitis → lymphatic spread from the focus

  • Hilar lymphadenitis → involvement of regional hilar lymph nodes

Langhans giant cells may be present histologically in a tuberculous granuloma, but they are not a component of Ghon’s complex itself.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ghon complex = Ghon focus + lymphangitis + hilar lymphadenitis

  • Ghon focus + involved hilar lymph nodes = Ghon complex

  • Calcified Ghon complex = Ranke complex

Exam Pearl:
Ghon’s complex is an anatomical primary TB complex—not a histological granuloma.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫৪) Complication of wound healing due to deficient scar formation is-
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Wound dehiscence is a complication of wound healing caused by inadequate/deficient scar formation, resulting in separation of previously approximated wound edges.

Other options:

  • Desmoid → excessive fibroblastic proliferation; related to abnormal scar-like tissue.

  • Hypertrophic scar → excessive collagen deposition within the boundaries of the wound.

  • Proud flesh → excessive granulation tissue, preventing epithelialization.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Complication Main defect
Wound dehiscence Deficient scar formation
Hypertrophic scar Excess collagen, stays within wound
Keloid Excess collagen extends beyond wound
Proud flesh Excess granulation tissue

Exam Pearl:
Deficient scar → wound dehiscence; excessive scar → hypertrophic scar/keloid.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫৫) All of the following causes generalized edema except……?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Generalized edema (anasarca) involves widespread accumulation of fluid in the interstitial tissues and is classically seen in conditions such as renal disease, liver disease, and severe malnutrition.

  • Famine edema → generalized edema due to severe protein deficiency/hypoalbuminemia.

  • Renal edema → generalized edema, especially in nephrotic syndrome.

  • Hepatic edema → generalized edema/ascites due to hypoalbuminemia and portal hypertension.

  • Angioedema → localized, acute edema of deeper skin/submucosal tissues, commonly affecting the face, lips, tongue, or airway.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Generalized edema → renal, hepatic, cardiac, malnutrition

  • Angioedema → localized, rapid swelling

  • Severe generalized edema → anasarca

Exam Pearl:
Generalized edema causes include renal, hepatic, and famine edema; angioedema is typically localized.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫৬) Which is the most common site for Crohn's disease?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The terminal/distal ileum is the most common site of Crohn’s disease. Crohn’s can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus, but the terminal ileum and ileocecal region are particularly common sites.

  • Stomach → uncommon.

  • Duodenum → uncommon.

  • Distal ileum → most common ✅

  • Rectum → less commonly involved; Crohn’s often spares the rectum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Feature Crohn’s disease
Commonest site Terminal/distal ileum
Distribution Skip lesions
Depth Transmural
Classic complication Fistula/stricture
Rectum Often spared

Exam Pearl:
Crohn’s disease → terminal ileum is the commonest site.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫৭) Which of the following is most characteristic of granuloma?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The epithelioid cell is the most characteristic and fundamental cell of a granuloma. Granulomas are organized collections of activated macrophages that transform into epithelioid cells, often surrounded by lymphocytes. Giant cells may form by fusion of epithelioid cells, but they are not essential in every granuloma.

  • Epithelioid cells → characteristic of granuloma ✅

  • Giant cells → may be present, but not always.

  • Fibroblasts → may contribute to fibrosis around chronic granulomas.

  • Endothelial cells → not a characteristic component.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Granuloma → epithelioid cells + lymphocytes ± giant cells

  • Epithelioid cells = activated macrophages

  • TB granuloma → caseation + Langhans giant cells may be present

Exam Pearl:
Most characteristic cell of a granuloma = epithelioid cell.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫৮) Krukenberg tumor is the metastatic gastrointestinal tumor to the......?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
A Krukenberg tumor is a metastatic ovarian tumor, classically arising from a gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma, most commonly gastric carcinoma. It typically consists of signet-ring cells containing mucin.

  • Ovaries → correct ✅

  • Umbilicus → Sister Mary Joseph nodule

  • Uterus → not Krukenberg tumor

  • Kidneys → not Krukenberg tumor

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Metastatic tumor Classic site
Krukenberg tumor Ovary
Sister Mary Joseph nodule Umbilicus
Virchow node Left supraclavicular lymph node
Blumer shelf Rectovesical/rectouterine pouch

Exam Pearl:
Krukenberg = metastatic gastric/GI signet-ring carcinoma → ovaries.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৫৯) Which blood group is mostly affected by carcinoma stomach?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Individuals with blood group A have a higher association with gastric carcinoma (carcinoma stomach) compared with other ABO blood groups. This is a classic epidemiological association frequently tested in medical exams.

  • Blood group A → increased risk of gastric carcinoma ✅

  • Blood group O → relatively lower risk of gastric carcinoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gastric carcinoma → Blood group A

  • Duodenal ulcer → Blood group O

  • Peptic ulcer disease → classically associated with blood group O

Exam Pearl:
Carcinoma stomach → think Blood group A.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬০) Which is the most common malignancy of the gastrointestinal tract?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Among the options, adenocarcinoma of the colon is the most common malignancy of the gastrointestinal tract. Colorectal carcinoma is predominantly adenocarcinoma and is a major cause of cancer morbidity and mortality worldwide.

  • Adenocarcinoma of colon → most common GI malignancy among these options ✅

  • Adenocarcinoma of stomach → common, but less common than colorectal carcinoma.

  • Cholangiocarcinoma → malignant tumor of bile ducts; relatively uncommon.

  • Barrett’s esophagus → a premalignant condition, not itself a malignancy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common histological type of GI malignancy → Adenocarcinoma

  • Common GI cancer site → Colorectum

  • Barrett’s esophagus → predisposes to esophageal adenocarcinoma

Exam Pearl:
GI malignancy + given options → colorectal adenocarcinoma is the best answer.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬১) All of the following causes pitting edema except…..?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Myxedema causes non-pitting edema due to accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (mucopolysaccharides) in the interstitial tissues, which bind water and produce a firm, doughy swelling.

In contrast:

  • Hepatic edema → pitting edema

  • Famine edema → pitting edema due to severe hypoalbuminemia

  • Renal edema → typically pitting edema

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Type Edema
Myxedema Non-pitting
Renal edema Pitting
Hepatic edema Pitting
Famine edema Pitting
Lymphedema Usually non-pitting

Exam Pearl:
Myxedema = non-pitting edema.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬২) Where heart failure cell is found?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages found in the lungs due to chronic pulmonary venous congestion, classically in left-sided heart failure. They are a characteristic feature of brown induration of the lung.

  • Brown induration of lung → heart failure cells 

  • Nutmeg liver → chronic passive congestion of liver due to right-sided heart failure.

  • Cardiac sclerosis → not associated with heart failure cells.

  • Strawberry gallbladder → cholesterolosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Heart failure cells → hemosiderin-laden macrophages in lung

  • Chronic pulmonary congestion → brown induration

  • Chronic systemic venous congestion → nutmeg liver

Exam Pearl:
Heart failure cells = hemosiderin-laden macrophages → brown induration of lung.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬৩) Which is a benign tumor of salivary gland?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Warthin tumor (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum) is a benign salivary gland tumor, occurring predominantly in the parotid gland. It is strongly associated with smoking and is usually slow-growing.

  • Warthin tumor → benign 

  • Adenocarcinoma → malignant

  • Adenoid cystic carcinoma → malignant

  • Mucoepidermoid carcinoma → malignant

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common benign salivary tumor → Pleomorphic adenoma

  • Second most common benign salivary tumor → Warthin tumor

  • Warthin tumor → parotid + smokers

  • Adenoid cystic carcinoma → notable for perineural invasion

Exam Pearl:
Benign salivary gland tumor among these options = Warthin tumor.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬৪) Accumulation of blood within tissue is called…..?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
A hematoma is a localized collection/accumulation of blood within a tissue or body space, usually caused by rupture of blood vessels due to trauma.

  • Hematoma → localized collection of blood in tissue 

  • Edema → accumulation of interstitial fluid

  • Hydrothorax → accumulation of serous fluid in the pleural cavity

  • Hyperemia → increased blood flow due to arteriolar dilation, not blood accumulation

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Blood in tissue → Hematoma

  • Blood in pleural cavity → Hemothorax

  • Blood in pericardial cavity → Hemopericardium

  • Blood in joint → Hemarthrosis

Exam Pearl:
Accumulation of blood within tissue = Hematoma.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬৫) Which is most common cause of thrombosis?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Stasis of blood flow is a major and very common contributor to thrombosis, particularly in venous thrombosis. It promotes thrombosis by causing endothelial activation/injury, allowing accumulation of clotting factors, and reducing the normal washout of activated coagulation factors.

The three major factors predisposing to thrombosis are Virchow's triad:

  1. Endothelial injury

  2. Abnormal blood flow — stasis or turbulence

  3. Hypercoagulability

  • Stasis → strongly associated with venous thrombosis 

  • High-speed/normal blood flow → generally protective against thrombosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:
Virchow triad = Endothelial injury + Stasis/turbulence + Hypercoagulability.

Exam Pearl:
For venous thrombosis, think stasis first.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬৬) Line of Zahn are marked in thrombi formed within….?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Lines of Zahn are alternating layers of platelets/fibrin (pale layers) and RBCs (dark layers) seen in a thrombus formed in flowing blood. They indicate that the thrombus formed before death (antemortem).

They are classically described in arterial and cardiac thrombi, where blood flow is relatively rapid. However, among the given options, aorta is the best answer—not veins.

So, the question is somewhat ambiguous if it expects the classic pathology distinction.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Lines of Zahn → antemortem thrombus

  • Pale layer → platelets + fibrin

  • Dark layer → RBCs

  • Best seen in arterial/cardiac thrombi

Exam Pearl:
Lines of Zahn = thrombus formed in flowing blood, classically arterial/cardiac.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬৭) Fat embolism is common in……?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Fat embolism most commonly occurs after fractures of long bones, especially the femur and tibia, because bone marrow fat enters the circulation after the injury.

  • Fracture of long bone → classic cause of fat embolism ✅

  • DVT → can cause pulmonary thromboembolism, not fat embolism.

  • Thrombophlebitis → may cause thromboembolism.

  • Blood transfusion → not a typical cause of fat embolism.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Fat embolism → long-bone fracture

  • Classical triad: respiratory distress + neurological symptoms + petechial rash

  • Usually develops 24–72 hours after injury.

Exam Pearl:
Long-bone fracture → think Fat embolism.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬৮) What type of hypersensitivity reaction occurs in anaphylactic shock?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Anaphylactic shock is a classic Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE.

On first exposure, the allergen causes IgE production, which binds to FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils. On subsequent exposure, the allergen cross-links IgE, causing rapid mast-cell degranulation and release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other mediators. This leads to vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, bronchoconstriction, and hypotension.

Other types:

  • Type II → antibody-mediated cytotoxicity

  • Type III → immune-complex mediated

  • Type IV → T-cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Type I → IgE → Mast cells → Anaphylaxis

  • Type II → IgG/IgM

  • Type III → Immune complexes

  • Type IV → T cells

Exam Pearl:
Anaphylactic shock = Type I hypersensitivity = IgE-mediated.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৬৯) Which is the most frequent cause of lung abscess?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The most common cause of lung abscess is aspiration of infected material, especially oropharyngeal secretions containing anaerobic bacteria. It is particularly associated with impaired consciousness, alcohol intoxication, anesthesia, seizures, or poor swallowing reflex.

  • Aspiration of infective materials → most common cause 

  • Septic embolism → can cause multiple pulmonary abscesses but is less common.

  • Neoplasia → may cause secondary infection/obstruction and abscess formation.

  • Primary lung infection → can cause abscess but is not the usual leading cause.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Lung abscess → aspiration is the classic/commonest cause

  • Common organisms → anaerobes from oral flora

  • Risk factors → alcoholism, impaired consciousness, dysphagia

Exam Pearl:
Lung abscess + most common cause → aspiration of infected oropharyngeal contents.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭০) Hemorrhage infarct doesn't occur in…….?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
A hemorrhagic (red) infarct occurs when blood can enter an area of ischemic necrosis, typically due to venous occlusion, dual blood supply, or reperfusion.

Common examples include:

  • Brain → hemorrhagic infarction can occur, especially after reperfusion of an ischemic area.

  • Twisted ovarian cyst → venous obstruction can produce hemorrhagic infarction.

  • Small intestine → venous obstruction can cause hemorrhagic infarction.

  • Kidney → usually produces a pale (white) infarct because it has an end-arterial circulation and dense tissue.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Red infarct: lung, intestine, ovary, brain (especially reperfusion)

  • White infarct: heart, spleen, kidney

Exam Pearl:
Solid organs with end-arterial supply → pale infarct; kidney is the classic exception to hemorrhagic infarction.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭১) Anesthetic accident produces…..?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
An anesthetic accident, particularly excessive spinal/epidural anesthesia or certain anesthetic-related injuries, can cause neurogenic shock due to sudden loss of sympathetic vascular tone. This produces widespread vasodilation, reduced venous return, and hypotension.

  • Neurogenic shock → loss of sympathetic tone; classically associated with spinal anesthesia or spinal cord injury. 

  • Anaphylactic shock → severe allergic reaction.

  • Septic shock → systemic infection.

  • Cardiogenic shock → pump failure of the heart.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Neurogenic shock → sympathetic loss → vasodilation + hypotension

  • Anaphylaxis → Type I hypersensitivity

  • Septic → infection

  • Cardiogenic → myocardial pump failure

Exam Pearl:
Anesthetic accident (especially spinal anesthesia) → neurogenic shock.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭২) Example of locally malignant tumor is…..?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Glioma is an example of a locally malignant tumor because it can show infiltrative growth into surrounding brain tissue, making complete surgical removal difficult. Some gliomas are highly malignant but generally have limited extracranial metastatic potential.

  • Glioma → locally infiltrative/malignant behavior ✅

  • Neuroblastoma → malignant tumor with metastatic potential.

  • Choriocarcinoma → highly malignant and rapidly metastatic.

  • Lipoma → benign tumor.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Locally malignant → infiltrates locally but has little/no metastatic tendency

  • Classic example → Basal cell carcinoma

  • Glioma → infiltrative growth within CNS

Exam Pearl:
Among these options, glioma is the best example of a locally malignant tumor.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭৩) Which one is the causative factor for genital warts?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Genital warts (condyloma acuminata) are caused by Human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly HPV types 6 and 11. These are considered low-risk HPV types because they are usually not associated with malignant transformation.

  • HPV 6, 11 → genital warts

  • HPV 16, 18 → high-risk types associated with cervical and other anogenital cancers

  • HSV → genital herpes

  • Treponema pallidum → syphilis

  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae → gonorrhea

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Genital wart → HPV 6 & 11

  • Cervical cancer → HPV 16 & 18

  • Genital herpes → HSV-2

  • Syphilis → T. pallidum

Exam Pearl:
Condyloma acuminata = HPV 6 & 11.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭৪) Which is Guardian of genome?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
p53 is known as the “Guardian of the Genome.” It is a major tumor suppressor protein that responds to DNA damage by:

  • Causing cell-cycle arrest → allows time for DNA repair.

  • Promoting DNA repair mechanisms.

  • Triggering apoptosis if the damage is irreparable.

The TP53 gene is one of the most frequently mutated tumor-suppressor genes in human cancers.

Other options:

  • RB1 → “Gatekeeper” of the G1 → S checkpoint.

  • SMAD4 → tumor suppressor involved in TGF-β signaling.

  • NF2 → tumor suppressor associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • p53 → Guardian of the genome

  • RB → G1/S checkpoint

  • APC → colorectal tumor suppressor

  • BRCA1/2 → DNA repair

Exam Pearl:
? p53 = Guardian of the Genome.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭৫) Kartagener syndrome excludes.....?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Kartagener syndrome is a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia caused by defective ciliary motility, classically due to a dynein arm defect.

The classic triad is:

  • Situs inversus 

  • Chronic sinusitis 

  • Bronchiectasis 

Cystic fibrosis is a different inherited disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene and is not part of Kartagener syndrome.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Kartagener syndrome Key feature
Situs inversus Present
Chronic sinusitis Present
Bronchiectasis Present
Defect Ciliary dynein
Cystic fibrosis Not a component

Exam Pearl:
Kartagener = Situs inversus + Sinusitis + Bronchiectasis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭৬) Cadmium is related to…….?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Cadmium exposure is an occupational/environmental carcinogen associated with an increased risk of lung carcinoma. It is encountered in industries involving battery manufacturing, metal smelting, welding, and pigments.

  • Cadmium → Lung carcinoma 

  • Arsenic → Skin, lung, and liver cancers

  • Aromatic amines → Bladder carcinoma

  • Benzene → Leukemia, especially AML

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Carcinogen Classic cancer
Cadmium Lung
Aromatic amines Bladder
Benzene Leukemia
Asbestos Mesothelioma + lung carcinoma
Vinyl chloride Angiosarcoma of liver

Exam Pearl:

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭৭) Which is the main site of colonization of staphylococcus aureus?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The anterior nares (nose) are the main site of colonization of Staphylococcus aureus. A significant proportion of healthy people carry S. aureus in their nasal passages without symptoms.

  • Nose/anterior nares → main colonization site ✅

  • Perineum → can also be colonized, but less characteristically.

  • Mouth → not the primary site.

  • Ear → not a typical major colonization site.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • S. aureus → anterior nares

  • Can colonize skin and perineum as well.

  • Nasal carriage increases the risk of self-infection and transmission.

Exam Pearl:
Staphylococcus aureus → anterior nares = main reservoir/site of colonization.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭৮) Grading of cancer is based on……?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Explanation:
Cancer grading is based primarily on the degree of differentiation of tumor cells and their microscopic features, such as cellular atypia and mitotic activity.

  • Degree of differentiation → determines grade ✅

  • Tumor size → contributes to staging

  • Lymph node involvement → staging

  • Distant metastasis → staging

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Term Based mainly on
Grading Degree of differentiation / histologic features
Staging Tumor size/extent + lymph nodes + metastasis (TNM)

Exam Pearl:
Grade = how abnormal/differentiated the cells look; Stage = how far the cancer has spread.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৭৯) Which group of herpes virus commonly causes congenital & perinatal infections?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
CMV (Human herpesvirus-5) is the most common congenital viral infection and is an important cause of congenital and perinatal infection.

Congenital CMV can cause:

  • Sensorineural hearing loss

  • Periventricular calcifications

  • Microcephaly

  • Growth restriction

  • Hepatosplenomegaly and jaundice

Other options:

  • HSV-1/HSV-2 → important causes of perinatal/neonatal infection, especially HSV-2 acquired during delivery, but CMV is the classic answer for congenital infection.

  • EBV → not a typical congenital infection.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Congenital infection → CMV

  • CMV → periventricular calcification + hearing loss

  • HSV-2 → neonatal herpes, commonly acquired during delivery

  • EBV → infectious mononucleosis

Exam Pearl:
Most common congenital viral infection = CMV.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮০) Which one is the most dangerous among 4 types of malaria?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
P. falciparum causes the most severe and potentially fatal form of malaria. It can infect RBCs of all ages, producing a high parasite burden and complications such as cerebral malaria, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, renal failure, and shock.

  • P. falciparum → most dangerous/severe 

  • P. vivax → usually less severe but can occasionally cause severe disease.

  • P. malariae → generally mild, chronic infection.

  • P. ovale → generally mild; can cause relapse.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most dangerous → P. falciparum

  • Cerebral malaria → P. falciparum

  • Relapse due to hypnozoites → P. vivax & P. ovale

  • Quartan fever (72 h) → P. malariae

Exam Pearl:
Falciparum = Fatal malaria.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮১) In DiGeorge syndrome hypoplasia or aplasia of which organ is seen?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
DiGeorge syndrome results from abnormal development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches, leading to thymic hypoplasia/aplasia and consequently T-cell immunodeficiency.

It is classically associated with CATCH-22:

  • Cardiac defects

  • Abnormal facies

  • Thymic aplasia

  • Cleft palate

  • Hypocalcemia

Other options:

  • Spleen → not the characteristic defect.

  • Liver → not involved.

  • Lymph nodes → may be poorly developed due to T-cell deficiency, but thymic aplasia is the key lesion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • DiGeorge → 3rd/4th pharyngeal pouch defect

  • Thymic aplasia → ↓ T cells

  • Hypocalcemia → parathyroid aplasia

  • 22q11 deletion → common genetic basis

Exam Pearl:
DiGeorge syndrome = thymic aplasia → T-cell deficiency.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮২) Which has association with HLA-B27?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
HLA-B27 has a strong association with ankylosing spondylitis (AS), a seronegative spondyloarthropathy affecting the sacroiliac joints and spine.

  • Ankylosing spondylitis → HLA-B27 ✅

  • RA → associated with HLA-DR4/DR1

  • SLE → associated with HLA-DR2/DR3

  • Osteomalacia → no characteristic HLA association

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • HLA-B27 → Ankylosing spondylitis

  • Also associated with reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, IBD-associated arthritis, and acute anterior uveitis

  • HLA-B27 is a risk factor, not diagnostic by itself.

Exam Pearl:
HLA-B27 → Ankylosing spondylitis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮৩) HCG is a tumor marker for……?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
β-hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) is an important tumor marker for gestational trophoblastic tumors, particularly choriocarcinoma and hydatidiform mole.

  • Trophoblastic tumor → β-hCG ✅

  • Carcinoma prostate → PSA

  • Pheochromocytoma → metanephrines

  • Seminoma → may have elevated β-hCG in some cases, but it is not the classic answer here; PLAP is a more characteristic marker.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • β-hCG → Choriocarcinoma / trophoblastic disease

  • AFP → Yolk sac tumor

  • PSA → Prostate carcinoma

  • CEA → Colorectal carcinoma

  • CA-125 → Ovarian epithelial carcinoma

Exam Pearl:
β-hCG = classic tumor marker for trophoblastic tumors, especially choriocarcinoma.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮৪) Which cytokine plays a central role in RA?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
TNF-α plays a central role in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). It is produced mainly by activated macrophages and promotes synovial inflammation by stimulating other inflammatory cytokines, endothelial activation, leukocyte recruitment, and joint destruction.

This is also why TNF inhibitors such as infliximab, adalimumab, and etanercept are important treatments for RA.

  • TNF-α → central cytokine in RA ✅

  • IL-1 → contributes to cartilage and bone destruction but is less central than TNF.

  • IL-2 → mainly involved in T-cell proliferation.

  • NO → inflammatory mediator, but not the principal cytokine.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • RA → TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6

  • TNF-α → major therapeutic target

  • Anti-TNF drugs → infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept

Exam Pearl:
TNF-α is the key cytokine driving chronic synovial inflammation in RA.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮৫) Spider web clot of CSF found in which type of meningitis?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
A “spider-web” or “cobweb” clot forms when CSF is allowed to stand in tuberculous meningitis. It results from a fibrin meshwork forming in the CSF due to the high protein content and chronic inflammation.

  • Tubercular meningitis → spider-web clot ✅

  • Bacterial meningitis → typically purulent/turbid CSF

  • Viral meningitis → usually clear CSF

  • Fungal meningitis → may have increased protein, but the classic exam association is TB meningitis

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • TB meningitis → spider-web clot

  • TB CSF → ↑ protein, ↓ glucose, lymphocytic pleocytosis

  • Bacterial meningitis → ↑ neutrophils, ↑ protein, ↓ glucose

  • Viral meningitis → lymphocytes, normal glucose

Exam Pearl:
?️ Spider-web clot in CSF = Tuberculous meningitis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮৬) Precancerous lesion of stomach doesn't include……?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Acute gastritis is not considered a precancerous lesion/condition of the stomach.

Recognized gastric precancerous conditions include:

  • Chronic gastric ulcer → associated with increased malignancy risk in some contexts.

  • Adenomatous gastric polyp → has malignant potential, especially larger lesions.

  • Pernicious anemia → associated with increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric neuroendocrine tumors.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gastric adenoma/adenomatous polyp → premalignant

  • Pernicious anemia → increased gastric carcinoma risk

  • Chronic atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma

  • Acute gastritis → not a precancerous lesion

Exam Pearl:
Acute gastritis does not constitute a precancerous gastric lesion.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮৭) Which is not a variation of RS cell?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
The Reed–Sternberg (RS) cell is the characteristic neoplastic cell of classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Recognized variants include:

  • Mononuclear variant → one nucleus/nucleolus.

  • Lacunar cell → characteristic of nodular sclerosis subtype.

  • Lymphocyte/histiocyte (“popcorn”) cell → characteristic of nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.

Nodular is not a morphological variation of the RS cell; it describes a pattern/subtype, not an RS-cell variant.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Classical RS cell → bilobed “owl-eye” nuclei

  • Lacunar cell → Nodular sclerosis

  • Popcorn/L&H cell → Nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL

  • Mononuclear variant → single nucleus

Exam Pearl:
Nodular = not an RS-cell variant; lacunar, mononuclear and L&H/popcorn are variants.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮৮) Which is not a feature of TOF?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) has four classic features:

  1. VSD

  2. Right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (usually pulmonary stenosis)

  3. Overriding aorta

  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy

So LVH (left ventricular hypertrophy) is not a feature of TOF.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • TOF = VSD + Pulmonary stenosis + Overriding aorta + RVH

  • RVH is expected, not LVH

Exam Pearl:
If it is TOF, think “right” ventricle hypertrophy, not left.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৮৯) Which one is the most important cause of NGU?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Chlamydia trachomatis is the most important and most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis (NGU). It is responsible for a large proportion of NGU cases, particularly in sexually active young adults.

  • Chlamydia trachomatis → most common/important cause of NGU ✅

  • Ureaplasma urealyticum → can cause NGU, but is a less consistent/secondary cause.

  • Trichomonas vaginalis → can cause urethritis, but is less common.

  • HSV → uncommon cause of urethritis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • NGU → Chlamydia trachomatis

  • Gonococcal urethritis → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

  • Another important NGU pathogen → Mycoplasma genitalium

Exam Pearl:
Most important cause of NGU = Chlamydia trachomatis.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৯০) Consolidation occurs in which stage of pneumonia?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
In lobar pneumonia, the classical pathological stages are:

  1. Congestion → vascular engorgement, edema, few neutrophils.

  2. Red hepatization → alveoli become filled with RBCs, neutrophils, and fibrin, producing firm consolidation. ✅

  3. Gray hepatization → RBCs disintegrate, with persistent fibrin and leukocytes.

  4. Resolution → enzymatic digestion and clearance of the exudate.

Thus, consolidation is classically established during red hepatization.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Stage Main feature
Congestion Vascular engorgement + edema
Red hepatization Consolidation + RBCs + neutrophils + fibrin
Gray hepatization RBC breakdown + fibrin
Resolution Clearance of exudate

Exam Pearl:
Lobar pneumonia → consolidation = red hepatization.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৯১) Which one is irreversible cell injury?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Necrosis is an irreversible form of cell injury, characterized by permanent cellular damage and death.

The other options are generally features of reversible cell injury:

  • Fatty change → reversible cellular injury ✅

  • Cellular swelling → classic reversible injury ✅

  • Cellular drinking (pinocytosis) → may occur as a reversible adaptive response

  • Necrosis → irreversible cell injury ✅

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Reversible injury Irreversible injury
Cellular swelling Necrosis
Fatty change Severe membrane damage
ER dilation Mitochondrial dysfunction
Ribosomal detachment Nuclear changes

Exam Pearl:
Necrosis = irreversible cell injury.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৯২) Focal cerebral infarcts are most commonly......?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
Focal cerebral infarcts are most commonly caused by embolism, particularly thromboemboli arising from the heart or large arteries.

  • Embolic → commonest cause of focal cerebral infarction ✅

  • Circulatory → cerebral infarction can result from systemic hypoperfusion, but this more often produces watershed infarcts.

  • Localized → not a specific etiologic category.

  • Fatty → fat embolism rarely causes cerebral infarction.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Focal cerebral infarct → embolism

  • Common sources → carotid arteries and heart

  • Watershed infarct → systemic hypotension/hypoperfusion

  • Embolic infarcts may show hemorrhagic transformation after reperfusion.

Exam Pearl:
Focal cerebral infarction → think embolism first.

Subject Final-04 Pathology.question: ৯৩) Which is not one of five subtypes of Hodgkin's lymphoma?
Subject Final-04 Pathology.exp:
